source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Part I: Breakouts: Transitioning into a New Trend

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: AlwaysInTrendContext
candidates.quote: “Always in” ... means that if you had to be in the market at all times, either long or short, the always-in position is whatever your current position is.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: a persistent regime state, whether the market's inferred ‘always-in’ direction is long or short. Used throughout the chapter to gate which side of a breakout is with-trend. Coded here as a simple EMA-side proxy; a real implementation may prefer a design-level always-in variable shared across chapters.

complexity.reason: ‘always-in’ is a persistent regime concept Brooks reserves for detailed treatment in book 3; any single-bar or EMA-side proxy is a design decision, not a direct mechanization.

notes: Every other RP1 candidate that says ‘in a bull trend’ or ‘in a bear trend’ depends on this primitive.

candidates.name: SignificantBreakoutBar
candidates.quote: A significant breakout ... almost always appears as a relatively large trend bar without significant tails.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the current bar is a large trend bar with small tails on both ends — Brooks's test for a breakout that is likely to have follow-through.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (high[0] - close[0]) <= tailFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (open[0] - low[0]) <= tailFraction * (high[0] - low[0])
notes: Brooks gives no numbers; bodyFraction and tailFraction are readings of ‘relatively large’ and ‘without significant tails’.
Reused verbatim as R08-01/02's LargeTrendBar in the gaps chapter; dedup pass should merge.

candidates.name: BreakoutPoint
candidates.quote: A breakout is simply a move beyond some prior point of significance such as a trend line or a prior high or low, including the high or low of the previous bar.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the bar closes beyond the highest high (or lowest low) of the prior N bars — the breakout point that later chapters remember and test.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the prior high (or a bull close for a close-based version)

complexity.reason: a highest-high window that degenerates to a single prior bar at lookback=1

notes: At lookback=1 this is exactly CloseAbovePriorHigh; larger lookbacks read as a swing-high breakout.

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackTest
candidates.quote: That point becomes the breakout point, and if the market later comes back to test that point, the pullback is the breakout test ... The space between the breakout point and the breakout test is the breakout gap.
candidates.description: After a breakout at bar b, a later bar's low returns to within the breakout-gap area around the remembered breakout point without trading meaningfully below it — the breakout pullback/test that many continuation entries buy.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= breakoutPoint + toleranceTicks * tickSize && low[0] > breakoutPoint - maxTestAtr * atr(atrLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: limit order to buy at or a tick or two below the breakout point

complexity.reason: breakoutPoint must persist as remembered state after the breakout bar

candidates.name: NestedRangeBreakoutFilter
candidates.quote: if you see that the current breakout is still below the high from 20 or 30 bars earlier, the market might still be in a trading range ... it is usually better to look to buy pullbacks instead.
candidates.description: Filter: only trust an upside breakout as the start of a new trend (buy the close / use a wide stop) once it also clears a much longer lookback high; a breakout that only clears a short lookback but sits below the wider-lookback high is more likely a breakout of a small range nested inside a larger one.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter distinguishing trend breakouts from range breakouts)

complexity.reason: a second, longer highest-high window compared with the breakout point

notes: A large enough wideLookback also approximates Brooks's ‘no bars overhead on the left side of the screen’ clear-path case (p30), which he treats as a green light to buy closes with a wide stop.

candidates.name: WeakBreakoutBarBlocksFollowThrough
candidates.quote: Bar 10 was a breakout of an ii bull flag, but the breakout bar was a bear reversal bar, which is a weak breakout bar. This increased the chances that the breakout would fail.
candidates.description: Filter: if the bar that made the breakout is not itself a significant trend bar in the breakout direction (e.g. it is a reversal or doji bar), treat the breakout as low-probability and withhold or reduce the with-trend entry.

complexity.reason: must identify the breakout bar and test its own bar quality one bar back

candidates.name: SpikeHeightMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: a strong breakout has at least a 60 percent chance of reaching a measured move that is approximately equal to the size of the spike
candidates.description: After a with-trend breakout spike, project a target beyond the breakout point equal to the height of the spike that produced it; exit (or take partial profits on) the long when the high reaches it.
candidates.pseudocode: spikeLow = lowest(low, spikeLookback)[b]; spikeHigh = high[b]; target = breakoutPoint + (spikeHigh - spikeLow); high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: target is frozen at the breakout bar; a lowest-low window otherwise

notes: Same construction as chapter 8's TradingRangeHeightTarget/SpikeHeightMeasuredMove (R08-13/R08-22); the dedup pass should merge these families.

candidates.name: FadeWeakReversalAgainstStrongerSpike
candidates.quote: Bar 22 was a strong bear trend bar in a bull trend, and many traders bought its close ... it was more likely that the bulls would outnumber the bears both below and above the bar.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, a bear trend bar whose range is small relative to the bull spike that preceded it is likely to fail as a reversal; buy at its close (or above its high).
candidates.pseudocode: AlwaysInTrendContext && close[0] < open[0] && (high[0] - low[0]) <= weakFraction * (highest(high, spikeLookback)[1] - lowest(low, spikeLookback)[1])
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the close of the bar, or above its high on a stop

complexity.reason: compares the current bar's range to a recent-range window; depends on the research-grade trend primitive

candidates.name: BearBarInBullTrendFirstTarget
candidates.quote: Their first target was a move to the high of the bar, which occurred two bars later
candidates.description: After buying the close of a bear bar per RP1-08, the first exit target is that same bar's high.
candidates.pseudocode: entryBarHigh = high[e]; high[0] >= entryBarHigh - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit at the entry bar's high

complexity.reason: the entry bar's high must persist as remembered state across subsequent bars

candidates.name: BearBarInBullTrendMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: the next target is a measured move up, equal to the height of the bear trend bar
candidates.description: Second exit target after RP1-09: project the height of the bear entry bar above its own high.
candidates.pseudocode: barHeight = high[e] - low[e]; target = high[e] + barHeight; high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: target is frozen from the entry bar's own range

candidates.name: ReversalBarVolumeMultipleConfirmation
candidates.quote: most bull reversals with protracted follow-through have about 5 to 10 times that volume, or at least 40,000 to 50,000 contracts.
candidates.description: Filter: a reversal bar's volume must be at least K times the N-bar average bar volume for the reversal to be considered reliable.

candidates.name: ReversalBarAbsoluteVolumeThreshold
candidates.quote: The most reliable bars have over 100,000 contracts.
candidates.description: Filter: a reversal bar's volume must exceed a fixed absolute contract count — a second, instrument-specific volume test distinct from the relative-multiple test in RP1-11.

complexity.reason: single-bar comparison against a fixed constant

notes: Emini-specific absolute figure; not portable across instruments without rescaling minContracts.

candidates.name: ChannelGapTestContinuation
candidates.quote: Once the market trades down to the area of the first of those channel bars, it often goes slightly below its low, and that puts the market in the gap area ... the test of the gap is usually followed by a resumption of the trend rather than the start of a reversal down.
candidates.description: After a breakout spike is followed by a tight trend channel, price testing back down into the area of (and slightly below) the first channel bar's low, while still in the with-trend regime, is a continuation buy rather than a reversal signal.
candidates.pseudocode: AlwaysInTrendContext && low[0] <= channelStartLow + toleranceTicks * tickSize && low[0] >= channelStartLow - maxUndershootAtr * atr(atrLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: buy at or slightly below the first channel bar's low

complexity.reason: needs channel-bar identification after a spike and a remembered start-of-channel low

candidates.name: ConsecutiveBuyClimaxesExpectCorrection
candidates.quote: it was the third consecutive bull climax without a correction since the bar 11 low ... consecutive buy climaxes often lead to a two-legged correction lasting about 10 bars
candidates.description: Filter: after the Nth consecutive buy climax (a bull spike with little or no intervening correction), stop adding to longs and expect a two-legged correction rather than immediate continuation.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter; take profits / stop adding rather than an order)

complexity.reason: ‘climax’ and ‘consecutive, without a correction’ have no agreed mechanical definition

notes: Related to R08-20's ClimacticConsecutiveTrendBarsExit, but counted at the climax/leg level rather than the single-trend-bar level.

candidates.name: TwoLegTenBarCorrectionMinimum
candidates.quote: The bulls didn't look to buy again ... until after the two-legged correction was complete
candidates.description: Filter: after a correction begins (per RP1-14), withhold new with-trend entries until at least minCorrectionBars have passed and minLegs legs of the correction have completed.

complexity.reason: leg counting has no agreed mechanical definition

candidates.name: TrendLineAndMABreakEnablesCountertrend
candidates.quote: Once the bears are strong enough to push a pullback well below the bull trend line and the moving average, they are confident enough that the market will likely not go much higher and they will aggressively short above the old high.
candidates.description: Filter: permit aggressive countertrend entries at the next test of the trend extreme only once a pullback has closed below both the trend line and the moving average (bull-trend case; mirrored for bear trends).

complexity.reason: needs trend-line projection from pivots plus an EMA comparison

notes: Combines the same trend-line-break idea as R08-15/R08-25 with an added EMA condition.

candidates.name: MinorTrendBreakoutWithinPullbackFade
candidates.quote: the minor bull trend will usually reverse back down into the direction of the major bear trend after breaking out above the first or second swing high in the pullback.
candidates.description: Filter: when a minor countertrend pullback within a larger trend breaks above (bear-trend case: below) its own first or second internal swing, do not buy that breakout — expect it to fail back toward the major trend.

complexity.reason: needs leg counting inside an in-progress pullback plus the outer trend context

candidates.name: ShrinkingTrendPullbacksIndicateMaturity
candidates.quote: Once a strong bull trend begins to have pullbacks that are relatively large, the pullbacks ... behave more like trading ranges than like bull flags ... a new high is now a breakout attempt above a trading range, and the odds are that it will fail.
candidates.description: Filter: once recent pullbacks within a trend grow beyond a fraction of ATR, treat the trend as maturing into a trading range and fade new-high/new-low breakouts rather than buy/sell them with-trend.

complexity.reason: ‘pullback depth’ and the maturity threshold require a design decision

candidates.name: BreakoutTestEntryAtPriorBarHigh
candidates.quote: if the breakout bar is not too large, the low of the next bar might test the high of the bar before the breakout, creating a breakout test. They might place a limit order to buy at or just above the high of that bar, and risk to the low of the breakout bar.
candidates.description: After a significant breakout bar, if the following bar's low comes back down to the high of the bar that preceded the breakout, buy there with a limit order and risk to the breakout bar's low.
candidates.pseudocode: SignificantBreakoutBar[1] && close[1] > high[2] && low[0] <= high[2] + toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: limit order to buy at or just above the pre-breakout bar's high; stop below the breakout bar's low

complexity.reason: a fixed three-bar structural test, but the risk level (breakout bar's low) is remembered state

rejected.quote: The best way for them to take a scary trade is to automatically trade only a third or a quarter of their normal trade size and use the wide stop that is required.
rejected.reason: position-sizing psychology heuristic, not a bar-level entry/exit test

rejected.quote: Every trading firm has its own measure of excess, and at some point enough firms decide that the trend has gone too far.
rejected.reason: pure discretion with no operational threshold given

rejected.quote: If the market goes up far enough above the breakout to enable a trader to make at least a profitable scalp before there is a pullback, then assume that there was mostly new buying at the high.
rejected.reason: a retrospective classification of what already happened, not a forward if-then decision rule

rejected.quote: As shown in Figure PI.2, the Emini was in a bear trend on the 60 minute chart on the left ... The 5 minute chart on the right reversed up after falling one tick below the 60 minute measured move target
rejected.reason: requires simultaneous multi-timeframe chart data (60-minute context for a 5-minute decision) that a single-timeframe bar series does not have

chapter_summary: Part I's introduction is conceptual rather than numeric: it defines breakout, breakout point, breakout test/gap, and 'always-in' as recurring primitives, then walks through how trend strength, pullback size, volume, consecutive climaxes, and trend-line/EMA breaks change which side of a breakout is worth trading. It produced the chapter's core primitives (RP1-01/02/03) that later ranges chapters (and the already-mined gaps chapter, R08) reuse, several concrete Entry/Exit pairs (fading a weak reversal bar and its two measured-move targets, a breakout-test limit entry, a channel-gap continuation), and a cluster of 'research'-grade context filters (climax counting, leg counting, trend maturity) that name real Brooks concepts with no settled mechanical definition yet.
